title: Life as a Shadow
english: the truth, so as to encounter unbelief. And he says again: 'and Ahaziah was swift in doing as the watchers in the field' (1 Kings 22:38). He was fast. And according to allegory, often the life of men and their polity is called a sea. Here, waves are able to signify what happens to man. And he says that regarding the judgments happening to him, 'it ascends even unto the heavens' and 'it descends even unto the depths' (Psalm 36:9).

[Gaps] ... in the following year ... [Gaps] ... what is superfluous to man? ... so in general regarding man he says, [Gaps] ... of the things ... [Gaps] ... when [Gaps] ... [Gaps] ... here also regarding [Gaps] ... the Jews were stronger ... [Gaps] ... the words of God and ... 'a part of him'. And those from the Greeks who believed were called ... [Gaps] ... the Jews being such as being a holy commonwealth and the others, but having made the things called [Gaps] subject to those on whom he was called ... and so this is to say 'what is superfluous', if first someone is called and ... [Gaps] ... he took it for himself ... [Gaps] ... [Gaps] ... and he speaks about the conduct and life here. This living we have while being in the flesh and passing through this. It is under time, it is under the number of days. But the truly living is eternal; and such a life is both eternal and without end. He speaks therefore about the life here, the life in heaven. And he made them in shadows; for who will announce to man what will be after him under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:9). The life of men, which they lead here, is shadowy. You have in the Gospel said by the Savior: 'Seek', he says, 'first the righteousness...'

"...and the kingdom of God, and all these things will be set before you." It is impossible for a shadow to be without a pre-existing body. There must be a body so that a shadow may thus follow it. Therefore, the life here is a shadow, being a consequence of a preceding life, which the life occurring here follows. For this reason it is said, "our days are as a shadow." And Job also said previously, "the life of men on the earth is a shadow." The life on the earth, or the material life, the temporal, the one in the flesh, this is a "shadow" of the life above.

It is a possible thing, an easy thing, a productive thing. So also the apostle, wishing to show the shadowy life, said, "If in this life we have only hoped, we are more to be pitied than all men" (1 Cor 15:19). Let a man, having some hope, attend to a shadow appearing to help him; in a palace, if someone perceives the face of a king not present, will the shadow or the appearance benefit him? For it is not possible for that which can be present to him beside a true king who rules according to laws, to be [the shadow itself]. Therefore our life is shadowy. But having known this, beloved, that this life is shadowy, attend to it as to something not permanent, as to something dependent on another; and in this, observe that there is another life which the shadowy life follows, and live and act according to that.

For thus "one is able to please God." Because of "who will announce to man" (Eccl 1:3) what follows him while he still exists under the sun, all divination is refuted from that source, all human prophecy. For "under the sun" is not in vain. For those having ascended above the sun of the Son and having approached the sun of righteousness, as it is said of them that "they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father," it is not possible to announce "what will come after," or what receives them. And as I have said and now will say: we say that we have ignorance of the judgments of God, since they happen to be "unsearchable. The judgments of God are very deep" (Rom 11:33). And the abyss is incomprehensible or difficult to comprehend. And let it be said that even if some were judged by a most righteous king in a dream, each according to his own sin, we all know that they were judged justly, though not to this extent...

title: The Good Name and the True Light
english: For what reason? We have this to say even here. Again, many among the rulers turned toward private interests. This same Ecclesiastes says: 'I saw slaves on horses and rulers riding about' (Eccl 10:7), and we cannot say for what reason he has this. But we can say in general that the things of men fall away. If, however, surpassing these, we become heavenly, no longer observing the temporal and apparent things, then we will lift ourselves to God, being able to know such things as follow after these.

For each one receives a reward according to his practice and his work. This is said regarding God by the Psalmist: 'You will render to each according to his works' (Ps 62:11). And even if the works are manifest, we do not trust in what kind of disposition is performing them. Moreover: 'And he made them in shadow.' The upward leading? He says this: 'Those having shone like the sun in the kingdom of their own Father' lived in the true days. In a manner of promising, he spoke concerning someone: 'I will fill him with length of days' (Dan 12:2). Indeed, these long days occurring toward the light of the truth are not shadowy; they are the prototypes. But the days which we can still receive while surrounded by flesh are shadowy.

Then one knows 'in part,' when 'the perfection has not yet come' (1 Cor 13:12), when he possesses the 'earnest of the Spirit' (Eph 1:14) and the light of the truth. Someone 'made these days in shadow,' but he did not know what would be behind him, whether he would surpass the shadow or fall down by it. And so that we may take the view from another example: the Jews have come to be in shadow, 'in the shadow' of days, not in the days themselves. For Moses, speaking the previous and true days, interprets: 'This is your life and this is the length of your days: to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5).

But the love toward God occurring 'from all the soul and from all the disposition' does not work an increase of these days. For many diligent and God-fearing men were quickly transferred from life, and others, the most mediocre, lived long. For who will announce to man what will be behind him under the sun? 196 Being of doubt...

One must take the word in two ways, so that this is both 'what shall be announced to him under the sun' (Ecclesiastes 1:9) and 'who else under the sun is able to announce'. Both are true. Furthermore, what is the leading up? This leading up is this: for both the man and the one striving to truly possess what is pleasant to him, [it is asked] 'who will announce to him, what will be after him under the sun'. It can be said here of the things that shine forth, those that lead up from the shadow, and those that guide from the temporal into the eternal. It is also possible to take this regarding the 'shadow' of righteousness, that 'who will announce to him, what will be to them under the sun', while still approaching righteousness. For he is no longer under the 'sun of righteousness' himself, having surpassed the shadow and having become in that truth seeing it 'face to face' (1 Cor 13:12).

A good name is preferred over oil, and the day of death over a day of birth. It exhorts to attend to a good reputation. For it has been said: 'A good reputation is praised by bones' (Prov 22:1). And we are accustomed to say that the one attending to virtue has acquired a good name, and the one living shamefully receives a bad name. Therefore, one is exhorted to attend to reputation. For this name, which seems to be sweet like oil, is good. Furthermore, is the spoken word clear? Those living well in life seem to be praised—but this can be with slander; such as the rich man remembered after Lazarus, and the one who heard: 'Fool, in this night they require your soul from you (Luke 12:20). But what you have prepared, what will it be?' Therefore, you prefer and choose this name of the seemingly good oil. But it is possible to take up the beautiful name, to make use of the chosen name of God. In order that the name not be bare, the good name consists according to virtue. And someone acquires this with toil and pain and sweat. But that which becomes sweet by chance often happens and is outside of their own striving. This is what the saint rejects, saying: 'Let not oil that sins anoint my head', which they think is sweet and oils themselves, but he says let it not be for me. For not every reputation is praiseworthy. The name here can be equal to reputation. Many are well-spoken of, who are able to exhaust others, [claiming] that they are rich, that they are rulers. This...

title: The Purpose of Mourning
english: Therefore the name is not for the sake of mercy. For there is nothing else of mercy. But that which is truly to be chosen and brings to the possessor something beyond the pleasures of life is the true name.

Similarly he speaks concerning days, that those truly bringing the things of importance according to the inner man and those leading an 'unblemished life' (βίον ἀκηλίδωτον) have a good name. And this is that which is beyond mercy, beyond the pleasures.

But some acquire this name not from works, not from life, but from the pride and haste of certain [people]. That name is not more choice than mercy. One must have something to be pitied; but with this mercy, if he makes his life right, the true name, more choice, is to be preferred.

And the day of his death is preferred over the day of his birth. The day of birth is the beginning of tribulation and ill-doing. The day of birth introduces man into life, where there are many evils and bad things; but the day of death imposes an end upon the struggling life.

Therefore he who does not attend to the things at hand nor thinks great things upon them, but knowing that 'it is better to be dissolved with Christ' (κάλλιον ἀναλύσαντα σὺν Χριστῷ εἶναι), prefers the day of death over the day of birth. For the one is the beginning of many evils, but the other is the end and the description of the evils.

And the evils we call here those of struggle, the indifferent things: poverty, vainglory, and those related to these. It is good to go into a house of mourning or to go into a house of wine (Ecclesiastes 7:4). Fluidity of character does not occur where mourning is. For there, boasting and laughing are turned away; this misfortune does not allow this to happen.

And at times, when we guard ourselves from misfortune through displeasure toward the unfortunate and the suffering, we are even permitted to appear joyful. But in the house of wine, what happens is contrary, bringing lust and songs, being a symptom of a coarse life.

Therefore, it is 'good' for the wise 'to go into a house of mourning or into a house of wine' (Ecclesiastes 7:4). This drinking together, when no evil is brought, brings neither good nor bad. Or is it so that we might not receive 'mourning' that is false? But that which the Savior makes blessed.
And regarding the spoken word, let us say that to be with those undergoing misfortune does not harm. The house of mourning, declaring our nature entirely, provides a reminder that we...

Not only the first ones are unhappy, but we also possess mourning; for mourning is common. But the ascent: the house is one of mourning, where there are doctrines of moral sins and the punishments upon them. For hearing these things, men both mourn and lament over themselves. So what, then, is the good in mourning? For it brings blessedness. For 'blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted' (Matt 5:4). Mourning is a prelude and a beginning of comfort. But the Savior does not bless those who mourn in just any way. For sometimes they also fall away, even while the word says: 'Do not weep for one dead, nor mourn him; but weep with a weeping for the one departing from the presence of the Lord, because he will not return again' (Luke 23:28). This one is worthy of weeping. It is not necessary to mourn the one dead, but the one dead having fallen away from blessedness and eternal life. In many ways, one can mourn himself having become lost in sins, if he perceives it. And he is blessed, the one mourning himself, having made himself worthy of mourning and having fallen from the blessed life, so that he may be comforted. And he mourns others also, when he is a lover of children. Thus indeed Paul was saying: 'Not having entered, I shall mourn many.' 'Many' he says, those 'not having repented.' This one mourning does not mourn himself, but the others having been made dead, or rather his own children through discipline in any way.

And the house signifies a certain state and an ascent, not a place. He knew this, the end of every man, and the living one will give good to his heart. The one going into a 'house of mourning' knows that 'the end of every man' is to die. And if he knows that he will die, he will not think much of it, nor will he consider it a matter of great importance if he possesses such things which he is able to cast off having died—wealth, glory, rank—according to 'do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied, for he will not take all things in his dying' (Prov 23:17-18). And the living one will give good to his heart. To the living belongs the hunting of what seems good to himself. This is the pleasant.
